title: Olbers' Paradox: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
question: If the universe is infinite and full of stars, why isn't the whole sky as bright as the sun?
summary: A simple observation about the dark night sky turns out to encode deep facts about the size, age, and expansion of the universe.
content:
Step outside on a clear night and look up. The sky between the stars is black. This seems too obvious to be interesting—of course space is dark—until you do the math. If the universe is infinite, eternal, and roughly uniformly filled with stars, then no matter which direction you look, your line of sight should eventually hit the surface of a star. Every point in the sky should be as bright as the surface of the sun. The night sky should blaze like day. It doesn't. This is Olbers' Paradox, named for the 19th-century astronomer who popularized it, though Kepler and others had wrestled with it centuries earlier.

The Naive Argument

Picture shells of space at increasing distance from Earth, like layers of an onion. A shell twice as far away contains four times as many stars (since its area grows with the square of distance), but each of those stars appears one-quarter as bright (since brightness falls off with the square of distance too). The two effects cancel exactly. Every shell, near or far, contributes the same total light to the sky. Add up infinitely many shells and you get infinite brightness—or at least a sky saturated with starlight, with no dark gaps at all.

Why It Doesn't Happen

The resolution isn't one clever trick but a stack of real physical facts, each of which chips away at the paradox's premises. The universe is not infinitely old: it began about 13.8 billion years ago, so light from stars farther than about 13.8 billion light-years hasn't had time to reach us yet. The universe is also expanding, and that expansion redshifts light from distant, receding galaxies out of the visible spectrum and drains its energy, dimming what does arrive. And stars themselves are not eternal—they burn for finite lifetimes measured in millions to billions of years, so the universe hasn't existed long enough, nor have enough generations of stars lived and died, to fill every line of sight with a luminous surface.

Put together, these facts mean our observable universe is a finite bubble of finite age containing a finite, imperfectly packed density of light sources. Most lines of sight simply run out of universe—or run into the cosmic microwave background, the redshifted afterglow of the Big Bang itself—before they hit a star.

A Paradox That Did Real Cosmological Work

What makes Olbers' Paradox remarkable is that a question you could ask while camping turns out to rule out entire classes of cosmological models. A genuinely infinite, static, eternal, uniformly star-filled universe is simply incompatible with a dark sky. Long before anyone had measured the cosmic microwave background or established the expansion of the universe with certainty, the dark night sky was already quiet evidence that the universe must have a beginning, or be expanding, or both. It's a rare case where armchair reasoning about something as mundane as darkness after sunset anticipated conclusions that took another century of technology to confirm directly.

What's Still Interesting

The paradox also sharpens intuitions about infinity that trip people up elsewhere in physics and mathematics: infinite sums can converge or diverge depending on subtle details, and "infinite" is not the same as "everywhere equally dense" or "equally accessible." The night sky is dark not because the universe is small, but because light is not instantaneous, stars are not immortal, and space itself is stretching—three separate, unglamorous facts that together produce something as ordinary and profound as darkness.

perspectives.title: Astrophysics Perspective
perspectives.description: The finite age of the universe and finite stellar lifetimes mean most lines of sight never reach a star's surface before running out of luminous sources or hitting the cosmic microwave background.

perspectives.title: Cosmology Perspective
perspectives.description: Expansion redshifts and dims the light of the most distant sources, further suppressing the sky's total brightness beyond what a static universe would produce.

perspectives.title: History of Science Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox predates modern cosmology by centuries and shows how a simple empirical observation can constrain grand theories long before direct measurement is possible.

perspectives.title: Mathematics Perspective
perspectives.description: The paradox is a lesson in how infinite sums behave: naive intuition about infinite space filled with sources doesn't guarantee infinite or even large total brightness once real constraints are added.
